quizName: DMV Practice Test #16 20 Questions • Passing Score 16

questions.question: When riding a three-wheeled motorcycle or motorcycle with a sidecar, why should you not ride too far to the right of your lane?

options.text: Other drivers may not see you.
You will not be able to pass other vehicles as easily.
Other drivers may try to share your lane.
You may run off the road.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may run off the road.
questions.explanation: A sidecar sits on the right side of a motorcycle. If you ride too far to the right, the sidecar may go off the road. On a three-wheeled motorcycle, the rear right wheel may also leave the road if you get too close to the edge.

questions.question: If you cannot avoid hitting an object in the road, what should you do?

options.text: Speed up before contact.
Slow down before contact.
Lean the motorcycle.
Stay seated on the motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow down before contact.
questions.explanation: Slow down as much as you can before hitting the object. Keep your motorcycle upright. Rise slightly off your seat. Roll the throttle slightly to lighten the front end just before impact.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a cause of a motorcycle wobble?

options.text: Incorrect tire pressure
Improper loading
Unsuitable accessories
Uneven road

questions.correctAnswerText: Uneven road
questions.explanation: Most wobbles come from improper loading, unsuitable accessories, or incorrect tire pressure. Do not try to accelerate out of a wobble.

questions.question: How should you park a motorcycle next to a curb?

options.text: At a 90-degree angle with the rear wheel touching the curb.
At a 45-degree angle with the front tire touching the curb.
Like a car, with both wheels the same distance from the curb.
At the left edge of the space so drivers can see it better.

questions.correctAnswerText: At a 90-degree angle with the rear wheel touching the curb.
questions.explanation: Park your motorcycle at a 90-degree angle to the curb with your rear wheel touching it.

questions.question: Where should inexperienced riders position themselves when riding in a group?

options.text: Just behind the leader.
In front of the group.
At the back of the group.
Beside the leader.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This allows experienced riders to watch them without making the inexperienced rider lead the group.

questions.question: If your motorcycle has convex mirrors and you are not familiar with them, why should you practice using them?

options.text: Most people are not used to using mirrors.
Unlike flat mirrors, they make items look farther away than they really are.
Unlike flat mirrors, they make items look closer than they really are.
It can be difficult to remember to look at mirrors while riding.

questions.correctAnswerText: Unlike flat mirrors, they make items look farther away than they really are.
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors show a wider view of the road behind you than flat mirrors. However, they make objects look farther away than they actually are. Practice using your mirrors so you understand this difference.

questions.question: Where should a child passenger sit on a motorcycle?

options.text: In front of the operator.
Behind the operator.
They do not have to reach the footrests.
They should hold onto the motorcycle frame.

questions.correctAnswerText: Behind the operator.
questions.explanation: A child should always sit directly behind the operator. If a child sits in front, they may not balance properly and could interfere with the operator's control of the motorcycle.

questions.question: The center of a lane often has an oily strip from vehicles. Is this area safe for motorcyclists?

options.text: Never safe.
Usually safe, unless the road is wet.
Usually safe, unless it is sunny.
Always safe, no matter the weather.

questions.correctAnswerText: Usually safe, unless the road is wet.
questions.explanation: The oily strip in the center of a lane usually provides enough traction for motorcyclists when the road is dry. The strip is usually about two feet wide, so you can often ride to one side of it and still stay in the center of your lane.

questions.question: How far ahead should you activate your turn signal before turning?

options.text: 10 feet
25 feet
50 feet
100 feet

questions.correctAnswerText: 100 feet
questions.explanation: You must activate your turn signal at least 100 feet before you begin a turn. Use your arm signal or mechanical turn signal when stopping, turning, or changing lanes.

questions.question: Should you wear a leather jacket while riding on warm days?

options.text: No, it will make you too hot.
Yes, but take frequent breaks to cool off.
Yes, riding jackets are made to keep you cool in warm weather.
No, jackets get in the way of steering.

questions.correctAnswerText: Yes, riding jackets are made to keep you cool in warm weather.
questions.explanation: Riding jackets help prevent dehydration and protect you from injury in warm weather. Many jackets are designed to protect riders even when it is hot outside.

questions.question: What helps you ride safely on slippery surfaces?

options.text: Using only the front brake
Using both brakes
Using the center lane
Maintaining or increasing your speed

questions.correctAnswerText: Using both brakes
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, slow down and use both brakes. Avoid sudden movements. Stay away from the center of the lane and follow the tire tracks left by cars. Watch for hazards like oil spots and loose gravel.

questions.question: What does this signal mean?

options.text: Rest stop
High beams on
Turn right
Hazard

questions.correctAnswerText: Hazard
questions.explanation: When riding in a group, signals help riders communicate. When the lead rider extends their right leg, it means there is a hazard on the right side of the road.

questions.question: When preparing to pass a vehicle on the left, why should you ride on the left side of your lane?

options.text: The right side could be slippery.
It gives you the best view of hazards in the next lane.
People don't usually expect to be passed on their left.
It places you in the rearview mirror of the car in front of you.

questions.correctAnswerText: It gives you the best view of hazards in the next lane.
questions.explanation: Riding in the left portion of your lane increases your line of sight. This helps you see hazards and makes you more visible to oncoming traffic.

questions.question: Because motorcycles are small, they appear to be:

options.text: Traveling faster than they actually are.
Traveling more slowly than they actually are.
Not moving when they actually are.
Closer than they actually are.

questions.correctAnswerText: Traveling faster than they actually are.
questions.explanation: Because of their small size, motorcycles may look like they are traveling faster than they really are.

questions.question: If you must brake and swerve to avoid a hazard, what should you do?

options.text: Do one, then the other.
Do both at the same time.
Always apply the brakes first, then swerve.
Try instead to use only the brakes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do one, then the other.
questions.explanation: If you need to brake and swerve, do each action separately. You can brake first then swerve, or swerve first then brake. Never do both at the same time.

questions.question: If your front wheel begins to skid, what should you do?

options.text: Keep the front brake engaged and ride out the skid.
Keep the front brake engaged and release the rear brake.
Immediately release and re-engage the front brake.
Release the front brake and increase pressure on the rear brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Immediately release and re-engage the front brake.
questions.explanation: If your front wheel locks while braking, release the front brake completely right away. Then apply it again smoothly.

questions.question: If a small animal enters your lane while you are riding in traffic, what should you do?

options.text: Do whatever you can, including swerving into other lanes, to avoid hitting the animal.
Switch lanes as quickly as possible.
Stay in your lane.
Flash your lights to try to scare the animal.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay in your lane.
questions.explanation: Avoid hitting animals when you safely can. In traffic, stay in your lane. Swerving into another lane to avoid a small animal can cause you to hit another vehicle. Hitting something small is safer than hitting something big.

questions.question: Which is a poor reason to sound your horn?

options.text: A driver in the lane next to you is too close to the vehicle ahead of them.
A parked car has a person in the driver's seat.
You want people to look at your motorcycle.
You are passing someone who is in the street.

questions.correctAnswerText: You want people to look at your motorcycle.
questions.explanation: Use your horn to alert a vehicle or pedestrian that may move into your lane. Sound your horn when passing a vehicle, a person in a parked car, or a pedestrian or bicyclist in the street. Do not use your horn just to get attention.

questions.question: When riding, what should you do?

options.text: Turn your head and shoulders to look through turns.
Keep your arms straight.
Keep your knees away from the gas tank.
Turn just your head and eyes to look through turns.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn just your head and eyes to look through turns.
questions.explanation: Look through a turn toward where you want to go. Turn only your head, not your shoulders. Keep your eyes level with the horizon.

questions.question: When riding at night, what should you NOT do?

options.text: Use your high beam.
Use the headlights of vehicles ahead to help you see.
Be visible.
Ride only in the left portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride only in the left portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: When riding at night, use your high beam unless you are following or meeting another car. Use the headlights of other vehicles to help you see. Wear reflective materials to be more visible. Change your lane position as needed to see, be seen, and keep safe distance from other vehicles.
